## What's special about the auditory system? {visibility="hidden"}

::: {layout="[60,40]"}

![Kaas & Hackett (2000)](images/schematic-auditorysystem.png){fig-align="center" height='800'  .fragment}

![Van Essen et al. (1992)](images/schematic-visualsystem.png){fig-align="center" height='800'  .fragment}

:::

## What's special about the auditory system? {visibility="hidden"}

::: {layout="[60,40]"}

![Kaas & Hackett (2000)](images/schematic-auditorysystem_box-subcort.png){fig-align="center" height='800'}

![Van Essen et al. (1992)](images/schematic-visualsystem_box-subcort.png){fig-align="center" height='800'}

:::

::: {.notes}
So why should we focus on the subcortical parts of the auditory system? I said that those are the harder parts to investigate with MRI, right? Well, there’s actually a lot going on in the brainstem and thalamus, especially in the auditory system.
Two examples from primates show differences between the wiring of the auditory and visual systems. In the auditory system, the first 5 layers of the system are subcortical, and with some cross-talk between them, so some processing can pass through even more structures.
Meanwhile, in the visual system, there’s just one or two stages before hitting primary sensory cortex. Indeed, a lot of processing is already done by the retina itself. With other features extracted later in successively higher levels of visual cortex.
Whereas in the auditory system, there’s some basic frequency and sound level information pulled out by the cochlea, but some other features like location of sound sources are extracted in the brainstem.

BUT THE VAST MAJORITY OF OUR KNOWLEDGE COMES FROM ANIMAL STUDIES
:::

::::

::: {.fragment}
### But: small, deep brain structures are challenging to image.
:::

::: {.notes}
Across human behaviors, studying the brainstem is challenging.
- In vivo MRI limited by:
 - high resolution needed for small structures
 - decreased signal as voxels get smaller
 - decreased signal in brainstem
- Limited spatial information from EEG, MEG
- Some human histology studies (nuclei)
- Tracer studies (connections) only in animal models
:::

## In vivo functional MRI mapping {visibility="hidden"}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="27%" .fragment}
### 7 Tesla functional MRI (1.1 mm voxels)
- 168 natural sounds (1 s each): speech, voice, nature, tools, music, animals and monkey calls
- Sound > baseline contrast
- 10 healthy participants
- 2 hours per session
- Collected over 2 sessions
:::

::: {.column width="73%" .fragment}
![](images/SitekGulban2019/fig_invivo_statmaps_and_exvivo_vasculature.png){fig-align="center" height=900}
:::
::::
![](images/people/Omer-Faruk-Gulban.jpg){.absolute bottom=10 right=10 width="200" height="200"}

::: aside
Sitek and Gulban et al. (2019 *eLife*)
:::

::: {.notes}
Participants listened to 168 natural sounds (1 s long) coming from seven categories (speech, voice, nature, tools, music, animals and monkey calls) presented in silent gaps in between the acquisition of functional volumes and were asked to press a button every time the same sound was repeated. The experimental paradigm followed a rapid-eventrelated design in which sounds were presented with a mean inter stimulus interval of four volumes (minimum three maximum five volumes). The two sessions were identical and each session consisted of twelve functional runs and across the 12 runs each sound was presented three times (i.e. each sounds was presented six times across the two sessions). The 168 sounds were divided in four sets of 42 sounds, each set was presented in three (non consecutive) runs. As a result, the 12 functional runs of each session formed four cross validation sets each one consisting of nine training runs and three testing runs (i.e. 126 training and 42 testing sounds). Note that the testing runs were non overlapping across the cross validations. Catch trials (i.e. sound repetitions) were added to each run, and were excluded from all analyses.
:::

## Anatomical connectivity mapping {visibility="hidden"}

:::: {.columns  layout-valign="center"}

::: {.column .fragment}
### Diffusion-weighted MRI tractography
- Look at how MRI signal varies across directions of molecular motion 
- Since white matter constrains the motion of water molecules, we can infer orientation of white matter in each voxel
- Then traverse voxel-to-voxel to estimate pathways (*tractography*)
:::

## Seeing the auditory brainstem on everyday MRI scanners

![](images/people/MichelleMedina.jpeg){.absolute bottom=10 right=10 width="200" height="200"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.fragment}
#### The problem
- The auditory brainstem is small and deep, so its MRI signal is weak
- Specialized 7T scanners help, but most hospitals and research centers have 3T
:::

::: {.fragment}
#### The fix: multi-echo fMRI
- Standard fMRI uses one "exposure" setting, tuned for the cortex
- Multi-echo captures several exposures and combines them, **like HDR on your phone camera**
- Each brain region gets the exposure that suits it, and noise (breathing, head motion) is easier to remove
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Study:** 14 adults listened to 10 minutes of pop music; 3 returned for many repeat sessions
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/multiecho-vs-singleecho.png){fig-align="center"}
:::

::::

::: aside
Medina et al. (2026 *Hearing Research*)
:::

::: {.notes}
So far, everything I've shown used 7 Tesla MRI. 7T is becoming more common (Siemens Terra is FDA-approved), but 3T is what most clinics have.

- Multi-echo fMRI acquisition (UMinn CMRR)
  - Echo times = 13.40/39.5/65.6 ms
  - Repetition time = 2.2 s
  - Multiband factor = 2
  - Voxel size = 1.731×1.731×4 mm^3^
  - Whole-brain coverage (44 slices, FOV=180mm)
- Multi-echo optimal combination + ICA noise removal (`tedana`)
:::

## *Where* are motor signals integrated? Subcortically?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}
- If integration is **subcortical**:
  - Expect to see **FFR** differences between *self-generated* and *passive* sound
- Recorded FFRs to /da/ stimulus
  - *Active* condition: press a button to generate a sound
  - *Passive* condition: passive presentation of the sound
  - *Motor* condition: button press alone, to subtract out motor activity
- Collected data from 33 normal-hearing adults

# Open tools for the frequency-following response: FFRPrep

::: {.notes}
Open science: BIDS-formatted data + an open pipeline means any lab can reproduce the analysis. That matters for comparing FFRs across labs and, eventually, clinics.
:::

## FFRPrep: an open, standardized pipeline for FFR data

![](images/people/MaxChen.jpeg){.absolute bottom=10 right=10 width="200" height="200"}
![](images/people/PeerHerholz.png){.absolute bottom=10 right=220 width="200" height="200"}

::: {.fragment}
FFR studies use **inconsistent analyses, file formats, and data sharing**, which makes results hard to compare across labs (or clinics)
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{=html}
<div style="display:flex; gap:14px; margin:20px 0;"><div style="flex:1; background:#f1eef6; border-radius:12px; padding:18px 22px;"><div style="color:#665086; font-weight:700;">1. Validate</div><div style="font-size:0.75em; margin-top:6px;">Checks the dataset follows the BIDS standard</div></div><div style="align-self:center; font-size:1.6em; color:#665086;">&rarr;</div><div style="flex:1; background:#f1eef6; border-radius:12px; padding:18px 22px;"><div style="color:#665086; font-weight:700;">2. Preprocess</div><div style="font-size:0.75em; margin-top:6px;">Filter, re-reference, epoch, reject artifacts</div></div><div style="align-self:center; font-size:1.6em; color:#665086;">&rarr;</div><div style="flex:1; background:#f1eef6; border-radius:12px; padding:18px 22px;"><div style="color:#665086; font-weight:700;">3. Analyze</div><div style="font-size:0.75em; margin-top:6px;">Evoked responses, spectra, pitch tracking, SNR</div></div><div style="align-self:center; font-size:1.6em; color:#665086;">&rarr;</div><div style="flex:1; background:#f1eef6; border-radius:12px; padding:18px 22px;"><div style="color:#665086; font-weight:700;">4. Report</div><div style="font-size:0.75em; margin-top:6px;">Automatic HTML report for every participant</div></div></div>
```

:::

:::: {.columns .fragment}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/FFRPrep/ffrprep_command.png){fig-align="center" width="95%"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **One command** runs the whole pipeline
- Containerized and versioned, so results are reproducible
- Runs on a laptop or scales across a computing cluster
:::
::::

::: aside
Sitek, Chen & Herholz (OHBM 2026); [sitek.github.io/ffrprep](https://sitek.github.io/ffrprep)
:::

::: {.notes}
Each stage is a modular Nipype workflow. Parallelizes across task/run within a subject (--n_procs); for clusters, one call per subject (e.g., slurm job arrays).

Preprocessing: load BIDS M/EEG with pybids + MNE-BIDS; reference (average, Cz, or M1/M2); filter while preserving the FFR; epoch from BIDS events, with amplitude-based rejection.

Analysis: combined evoked, per-trial-type evokeds (e.g., positive/negative polarity), and difference evokeds.

Future: multi-channel validation, more denoising/artifact options, single-trial classification, more test datasets.

Max Chen (Cog Sci/Comp Sci undergrad) and Peer Herholz.
:::

## Every participant gets a transparent report: preprocessing

![](images/people/MaxChen.jpeg){.absolute bottom=10 right=10 width="200" height="200"}

![](images/FFRPrep/panel_average.png){fig-align="center" height="290" .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Top: the participant's average FFR (here, 1773 epochs) with SEM and stimulus onset.

Bottom: automatic quality checks for every epoch: peak-to-peak amplitude distribution with the rejection threshold, RMS across epochs (spots noisy stretches), SNR over time, an epoch-by-epoch heatmap, and the power spectrum (line noise, etc.).

## Every participant gets a transparent report: analysis

![](images/people/MaxChen.jpeg){.absolute bottom=10 right=10 width="200" height="200"}
![](images/people/PeerHerholz.png){.absolute bottom=10 right=220 width="200" height="200"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](images/FFRPrep/panel_tfr.png){fig-align="center" width="100%" .fragment}

![](images/FFRPrep/panel_xcorr.png){fig-align="center" width="100%" .fragment}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/FFRPrep/panel_pitch.png){fig-align="center" width="100%" .fragment}

::: {.fragment}
#### Try FFRPrep and let us know what you think!
:::
:::
::::

::: aside
Sitek, Chen & Herholz (OHBM 2026); [sitek.github.io/ffrprep](https://sitek.github.io/ffrprep)
:::

::: {.notes}
Time–frequency: energy at the stimulus f0 (~100 Hz) and harmonics during the sound.

Stimulus–response cross-correlation: how faithfully the brain response follows the stimulus waveform, and at what lag (here, peak at ~23 ms, consistent with subcortical generators).

Pitch tracking: f0 extracted from the response over time, colored by confidence; tracks the 100 Hz stimulus f0 during the steady-state portion.

Each report also includes waveforms, spectra, autocorrelation, phase consistency, and scalar metrics (RMS SNR, spectral power), for each condition and their differences.

Musicianship EEG Dataset (Whiteford et al., 2025, Nature Communications): 296 participants, 6 sites; we converted it to BIDS and shared it on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22967621). License: CC BY-NC 4.0.

Same /da/ syllable as the auditory–motor studies we just saw, so FFRPrep applies directly to our own data.
:::

# Auditory categorization in the human brain

::: {.notes}
Speaker notes go here.

## How do we learn new sensory categories?

::: {layout="[70,30]"}

::: {.incremental}
- **Dorsal striatum** contributes to learning new categories thanks to its projections from **distributed cortical networks** that perform:
  - motor planning
  - **task-relevant sensory processing**
  - **feedback processing**
  - decision-making
- Dorsal striatum involved in auditory category learning tasks using fMRI (Feng et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2016)
  - What **anatomical pathways** connect the human auditory system to the striatum?
  - How do *subdivisions* of dorsal striatum **functionally contribute** to category learning?
:::

![Lim et al., 2014](images/Lim_striatum-schematic.jpg){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: aside
This work is actively supported by K01-DC019421 (PI: Sitek)
:::


::: {.notes}
Speaker notes go here.
:::

## Each cortical network has its own striatal connectivity profile

![](images/Sitek_connectivity_network-comparison.svg){fig-align="center" height="560" .fragment}

::: {.incremental}
- **Auditory** and **visual** cortices connect most strongly with the **posterior putamen** – but auditory is more hierarchical
- **Prefrontal** cortex connects broadly across caudate and anterior putamen
- **Motor** cortex favors posterior putamen and posterior caudate
:::

::: aside
Sitek et al. (in revision); Human Connectome Project 7T diffusion-weighted MRI (n = 97)
:::

::: {.notes}
Diffusion tractography from each cortical network to four dorsal striatal subdivisions (aCAU, pCAU, aPUT, pPUT), both hemispheres. Note the log-scale y-axis: differences between subdivisions are often an order of magnitude.

Visual cortex follows the same posterior-putamen pattern as auditory.
:::

#### Striatum feedback responses 
  - All regions showed positive responses in *early* learning stage
  - But only **anterior putamen** *maintained* positive responses across all runs
  - Only **anterior caudate** *significantly decreased* responses from early to final learning stages

## Same sounds, different listeners: one group learns, one already knows

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.incremental}
- 6 runs, grouped into *early*, *middle*, and *final* learning stages
- **Learners** (non-Mandarin speakers) and **native Mandarin multilinguallisteners** hear the same sounds and do the same task, but natives have nothing to learn
:::
:::

::: {.column width="60%" .fragment}
![](images/Sitek2026_categorization/behav_acc_two-group.svg){fig-align="center" height="800"}
:::

::::

::: aside
Group × run *F*(5, 115) = 19.1, *p* < .001
:::

::: {.notes}
Natives are the control for everything except learning: same sounds, same responses, same feedback, but nothing to learn.

Learners rise from .38 to .82 (t(11) = 6.68). Natives are at ceiling: .95 in run 1, then ~.98.

If asked whether natives improved: small gain from run 1 to 2 (p = .041). That's getting used to the task, not learning the categories.
:::

## Learning reshapes the caudate's response to feedback

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/Sitek2026_categorization/striatal_trends_fbcorrect.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

::: {.fragment}
- Learners' anterior caudate starts *above* natives' and converges by the final stage
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
![aCAU − aPUT trend: difference = −0.66, *t* = −2.52, *p* = .019](images/Sitek2026_categorization/group-diff_key-results_aCAU-aPUT.svg){fig-align="center" height="650"}
:::

::::

::: {.fragment}
#### As learners learn, the anterior caudate's feedback response falls *relative to* the anterior putamen. Natives show no such shift.
:::


::: {.notes}
Within learners, aCAU's response to correct vs. wrong feedback declines with learning. Comparing groups requires correct feedback alone, because natives rarely make errors. On that contrast, the caudate-relative-to-putamen shift separates the groups.

Stage-by-stage gap (learners − natives, aCAU): +0.30, +0.15, −0.11. Present as convergence; no formal test.

Be clear: it's a *relative* difference. None of the four separate trends (aCAU and aPUT in each group) is significant, and the aCAU-only group test isn't either (p = .13).

Natives "flat": their aCAU trend is equivalent to zero (TOST q = .024), so "flat" is a tested claim, not a missing effect.

 (permutation *p* = .018; holds when any one participant is dropped)

:::

## Learners treat the sounds differently: frontal deactivation and weaker auditory responses

::: {.incremental}
- Both groups' auditory cortex and putamen respond to the tones
- But learners **deactivate medial frontal cortex** during sounds, and natives' **posterior STG** responds more strongly
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
#### Medial frontal cortex: lower in learners
::: {layout="[[64,36]]" layout-valign="center"}
![](images/Sitek2026_categorization/group-diff_network-pfc_contrast-sound_stage-averaged_medial.png)

![](images/Sitek2026_categorization/group-diff_key-results_FMC.svg)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
#### Posterior STG: stronger in natives
::: {layout="[[64,36]]" layout-valign="center"}
![](images/Sitek2026_categorization/group-diff_network-auditory_contrast-sound_stage-averaged_lateral.png)

![](images/Sitek2026_categorization/group-diff_key-results_STGp.svg)
:::
:::

::::

::: aside
Frontal medial cortex (FMC): *d* = −1.44, *q* = .013; posterior STG: *d* = −1.23, *q* = .036
:::

::: {.notes}
These differences weren't predicted, so present them as new observations. One possibility: the frontal deactivation reflects effortful listening to unfamiliar categories.

No group difference in lateralization (group × hemisphere p = .22).

STGp: FLT15 is now a confirmed valid participant, so q = .036 is the result. Still, say "stronger in natives" rather than leaning on it.
:::

## Auditory categorization in the human brain

:::  {.fragment}
#### We identified putative cortico–striatal pathways for auditory decision-making
- Primary/secondary auditory cortex connects more strongly with *posterior* dorsal striatum
- Non-invasive human connectivity is similar to invasive tracing in non-human primates (Yeterian & Pandya 1998)
- Auditory connectivity is similar to visual connectivity, but more hierarchical; prefrontal connectivity is more distributed
:::
::: {.fragment}
#### Comparing learners with native listeners isolates learning
- Learning shifts the **anterior caudate**'s feedback response relative to the **anterior putamen**
- Learners deactivate **medial frontal cortex** during sounds; natives' **posterior STG** responds more strongly
:::

### Putamen and caudate *subdivisions* have unique functional and connectivity profiles {.fragment}

::: aside
Sitek et al. (in revision)
:::

## Sensory *and motor speech* learning: Shared striatal mechanisms?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Dorsal striatum (caudate and putamen) is critical to auditory learning (Sitek et al., in revision) *and* motor learning
- Are the neural implementations shared across perceptual and motor learning **in the context of speech and language**?
- How are shared mechanisms affected in *stuttering* or *Parkinson's*, and can they **inform therapeutic opportunities**?

:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![Lim et al., 2014](images/Lim_striatum-schematic.jpg){fig-align="center"}

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Stuttering Treatment implications
Learning-based therapy, not just fluency shaping
Emphasize rewarded, gradually stabilized speech patterns
Closed-loop auditory reinforcement paradigms
More targeted dopamine modulation (dose, timing, task-coupled)
Neurostimulation aimed at striatal–SMA loops, not just cortex

Dyslexia Treatment implications
Shift from pure phonics to reinforcement-based learning frameworks
Use adaptive reward schedules to strengthen sound–action associations
Predict differential benefit from procedural vs declarative training
Early identification via auditory category learning tasks, not just phonological tests

Parkinson's Treatment implications
Therapy timed to dopaminergic state to optimize learning
Use of external reinforcement and cueing to replace striatal learning
Personalized speech therapy based on learning rate, not just severity
Speech as a biomarker for basal ganglia learning capacity

:::

## Hearing our own speech: *Where* are motor signals integrated in auditory cortex?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Auditory cortex is a hub for motor integration
- But fMRI often shows *increased* BOLD to self-generated sounds, vs. *suppressed* M/EEG
- Are different **laminar** responses the explanation? 

#### We can look at intra-cortical circuits with ultra-high field **7T fMRI** {.fragment}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![Behroozmand et al. (2015)](images/Behroozmand%202015_sp-gt-play_no-shift.png){fig-align="center" height="150"}

![Reznik et al. (2015)](images/Reznik2014_Figure1a.png){fig-align="center" height="150"}

:::
::::

::: aside
:::

::: {.notes}
Behroozmand (2015) discussion para 2:
> When compared to rest, we found that during both speaking and playback conditions, the strongest activation in response to normal (no shift) and pitch-shifted vowel sound was observed within temporal lobe auditory cortices. This temporal lobe activation did not differ significantly for the speaking versus playback conditions. However, during speaking, we found significant BOLD activation increases in other sensory–motor areas including bilateral precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus, anterior insula, SMA and IFG compared with playback. The speaking-induced BOLD response enhancement in these sensory–motor areas was not significantly modulated by the presence or absence of pitch-shift stimulus in the auditory feedback.

:::

## Hearing our own speech: *Where* are motor signals integrated in auditory cortex? {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Auditory cortex is a hub for motor integration
- But fMRI often shows *increased* BOLD to self-generated sounds, vs. *suppressed* M/EEG
- Are different **laminar** responses the explanation? 

#### We can look at intra-cortical circuits with ultra-high field **7T fMRI**

::: {.incremental}

- **Cortical depth profile** differences during self-generated vs. passive sound listening
- Higher increases at **superficial** cortical depths, suggesting increased **corticocortical** feedback
- Future work: Pinpointing feedback dysfunction in *stuttering*, *schizophrenia*, and other feedback processing disorders
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

#### Auditory processing changes throughout adulthood
- How does speech-in-noise processing change in middle age and beyond?
- What neural patterns predict later cochlear implant success?

::: {.fragment}
#### Speech processing in the developing brain
- How do children make auditory category decisions, and how are they affected by noise?
- What compensatory neural pathways are available to children with developmental communication differences?
:::
:::

## Enhancing clinical precision with stronger human neuroscience {visibility="hidden"}

### Established collaborations
- Functional and structural connectivity in **persistent developmental stuttering** (Sitek et al., 2016; ongoing Pitt collaboration)
- Speech feedback control in individuals with **cerebellar stroke** (R01 Co-Investigator; PI: Bohland)
- White matter pathways in **autism spectrum disorder** (Boets et al., 2018)
- White matter integrity in **sensorineural hearing loss** (Tarabichi et al., 2018)

### R01 proposal: Neurobiology of middle-aged hearing loss
- *Basic neuroscience*: Quantify the relationship between noise exposure, hearing-in-noise difficulty, and structural changes to the cochlea, nerve, and cortex (in an animal model; Aravind Parthasarathy, Pitt)
- *Human neuroscience*: Identify structural, metabolic, and brain network relationships with noise exposure and speech-in-noise challenges (**Kevin Sitek**, imaging center TBD)
- *Translational neuroscience*: Develop speech-in-noise metrics and clinically applicable EEG to identify early hidden loss and provide therapeutic opportunities (Bharath Chandrasekaran, Northwestern Center for Speech, Hearing, and Language Learning)

# Extra slides {visibility="uncounted"}

## How do kids learn to hear in noisy environments? {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {layout-ncol=2  layout-valign="bottom"}

::: {.incremental}
- Adults listening in noise rely on speech networks *plus* extra motor and prefrontal "helper" regions^[Du et al. (2014); Vaden et al. (2013); Eckert et al. (2016)]
- In children, speech networks are still fine-tuning, and frontal networks are still developing
- **Study:** 35 typically developing kids identified syllables in quiet and in increasing background noise (3T fMRI)
:::

![via The Telegraph](images/Cocktail-party.jpg){fig-align="center"}

:::

::: aside
Sitek et al. (in prep.; SNL 2025)
:::

::: {.notes}
Design: 5 speech-shaped noise contexts (Quiet and SNR = +8, 0, -2, -6); identify which of 4 syllables was presented.
:::

## Speech-in-noise systems are still developing in adolescents {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {layout="[40,60]"   layout-valign="bottom"}
::: {.incremental}
- Kids activate auditory and language regions more strongly for clear than for noisy speech
- But no sign yet of the extra motor and prefrontal "helper" regions adults use in noise
:::

![](images/Sitek_SSP_quiet-gt-n6.png){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: aside
Sitek et al. (in prep.; SNL 2025); Hampton-Wray R01DC019904
:::

::: {.notes}
Figure: speech-in-quiet vs. -6 dB SNR.

Next: investigating task-relevant *representations* in development.
:::

Speaker notes go here.
:::

## Same data, new statistics: Mapping finger representations with Bayesian random partition models

- New Bayesian hidden Markov random partition model maps how an effect's pattern *and* size vary locally across the brain
- Applied to button presses during the 7T auditory category-learning task (1 participant, 6 runs)
- Finger-specific representations across sensorimotor cortex, cerebellum, and dorsal striatum


::: {layout-ncol=3}
![](images/Moya_etal_2025/dmncADL.png)

![](images/Moya_etal_2025/dmncADR.png)

![](images/Moya_etal_2025/dmncPVR.png)
:::

Posterior mean dominance greater than 25% across voxels for the [right index  (red)]{style="color:red;"}, [left index (blue)]{style="color:blue;"}, and [middle fingers (green)]{style="color:green;"}. 

![](images/people/BlakeMoya.jpeg){.absolute bottom=10 right=10 width="200" height="200"}
![](images/people/AbhraSarkar.png){.absolute bottom=10 right=220 width="200" height="200"}

::: aside
Moya et al. (2026 *arXiv*: [2609.13319](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.13319))
:::

::: {.notes}
Collaboration with Abhra Sarkar (UT Austin) and Blake Moya (former UT Austin PhD student), using the striatal learning dataset to develop a new statistical technique.

Results for the fingertip mapping study:     
Fingertip dominance across the investigated regions. Posterior mean dominance greater than $25\%$ is shown across voxels for the right index finger (red), left index (blue), and middle fingers (green) based on the estimated partition structures and the estimated effect intensities.     
Colors blend when two or more fingers exhibit greater than $25\%$ dominance probabilities at the same location,     showing areas of competing dominance for the right index and either middle finger (yellow), left index and either middle finger (cyan), and the two index fingers (purple).
:::
